title: Cloud Engineer & SRE
summary: Master real-world infrastructure incidents, cloud telemetry, CI/CD regressions, and post-mortem investigations.

industry_glossary.definition: A target percentage (e.g. 99.9% uptime) that a service team commits to maintaining.
The 99th percentile response time—meaning 99% of requests are faster than this number, highlighting worst-case user experiences.
Server-side error codes (500 Internal Error, 502 Bad Gateway, 504 Gateway Timeout) indicating system-level crashes or upstream timeouts.
Deploying a new software version to a tiny subset of traffic (e.g., 2%) to observe error rates before rolling out globally.
When all available database or network connections are occupied, forcing incoming requests to queue and eventually time out.

common_tools.name: Kubernetes & Helm
common_tools.description: Used to deploy containerized services, manage rolling releases, and execute instantaneous rollbacks during incidents.

common_tools.name: Prometheus & Grafana
common_tools.description: Aggregates time-series performance metrics, tracks p95/p99 percentiles, and alerts when error thresholds breach SLOs.

common_tools.name: Datadog & OpenTelemetry
common_tools.description: Provides end-to-end distributed tracing across microservices, isolating connection bottlenecks and thread starvation.

common_tools.name: PagerDuty
common_tools.description: Automates on-call paging, Sev-1 incident mobilization, and incident war room communication.

standard_workflows.summary: Alert fires via PagerDuty; on-call engineer acknowledges within 5 minutes and verifies scope of customer impact.
Prioritize rapid service recovery over debugging. Revert bad commits via Helm rollback or disable risky toggles via feature flags.
Monitor p99 latency and 5xx error rate for at least 15-30 minutes to confirm stabilization across all pods.
Draft a timeline, identify systemic technical vulnerabilities, and schedule preventive engineering tasks to eliminate recurrence.

readiness_quiz.question: An alert fires showing p99 latency jumped from 150ms to 4,000ms right after a release. What is the safest first step?
options: A) SSH into the production database and delete slow queries manually
B) Check recent deployment diffs, error logs, and assess whether a rollback or canary drain is warranted
C) Wait 30 minutes to see if traffic naturally subsides
D) Increase server CPU limits without checking why latency surged
readiness_quiz.explanation: Checking release diffs and assessing rollback options stops ongoing user impact fastest, minimizing Mean Time to Recovery (MTTR).

readiness_quiz.question: What is the primary difference between a fact and an assumption in an incident report?
options: A) A fact is supported by direct telemetry or log timestamps; an assumption is a hypothesis that needs verification
B) Facts are written by junior engineers; assumptions are written by senior engineers
C) Facts always blame third-party vendors
D) There is no difference in fast-paced incident calls
readiness_quiz.explanation: Clear distinction between verified signals (logs, metrics) and unconfirmed hypotheses prevents teams from pursuing dead-end rabbit holes.

readiness_quiz.question: Why is an immediate rollback usually preferred over a quick 'hotfix' patch during an active critical outage?
options: A) Rollback returns the service to a known stable state without risking unvetted changes under emergency pressure
B) Hotfixes are illegal in modern DevOps
C) Rollbacks never require testing
D) Rollbacks erase the Git commit history permanently
readiness_quiz.explanation: Writing and deploying code under outage pressure frequently introduces secondary bugs. Rolling back to a proven build is safer.

readiness_quiz.question: What signal best confirms that a high-latency incident has truly resolved?
options: A) The on-call engineer closes the Slack thread
B) Both error rates and p99/p95 latency metrics return to baseline levels for at least 15-30 minutes across all nodes
C) A single test curl request returns HTTP 200 OK
D) The CPU usage drops to 0%
readiness_quiz.explanation: Sustained observation across all metric percentiles and instances confirms recovery, whereas a single HTTP 200 could be a fluke.

readiness_quiz.question: What is the primary purpose of a post-incident review (post-mortem)?
options: A) To identify which individual engineer made the mistake and penalize them
B) To conduct a blameless analysis, identify systemic weaknesses, and implement preventive guardrails
C) To convince customers that nothing went wrong
D) To document why writing tests is optional
readiness_quiz.explanation: Blameless post-mortems focus on process and technical resilience so the entire organization learns from failures.
